content.title: Event Data: Know What Happened
content.hook: Sometimes knowing that an event happened is not enough. The handler may need information about what happened.
content.context: Sometimes knowing that an event happened is not enough. The handler may need information about what happened.
goals: Use the event object and `event.target` to identify the element involved in an interaction.

content.title: The event object

content.question:
Suppose this page has one button:

```html
<button id="save">Save</button>
```

When that button is clicked, what should `event.target` refer to?

feedback.correct: Correct answer: A. The button element
feedback.incorrect: Correct answer: A. The button element

content.title: Multiple buttons
content.text:
Imagine three buttons:

```html
<button>One</button>
<button>Two</button>
<button>Three</button>
```

Each button can use the same idea. The event tells the handler which element was involved in that particular click.

content.title: Try it
Important limitation
content.text:
`querySelector(".choice")` selects only the first matching button. The example is intentionally small so you can see the event data clearly.

Handling many matching elements is a separate design problem we can solve later.

content.question: What is the main job of the event object in this lesson?

options.text: It contains information about the event that just occurred.
It stores every element on the page forever.

feedback.correct: Correct answer: A. It contains information about the event that just occurred.
feedback.incorrect: Correct answer: A. It contains information about the event that just occurred.

content.title: Forge takeaway & Lesson completion
takeaways: **Mental model:** An event tells you that something happened; the event object can tell you more about what happened.
**Senior habit:** Before writing a handler, identify what information the handler actually needs.
